question: Who looks at the live service to get the five facts that the record does not have?
context: A read is a look at the live service that changes nothing. Example: your answer to D-LOAD-02 moves the Worker near the database, but nobody knows where the database runs. One command prints that place and reads no table. The audit made no such look, so five facts of the record are assumptions. On 2026-10-07 you authorized the implementation and two writes to production D1. You did not name the reads. A read uses your Cloudflare login. That login can also write, and the account has other projects. The table before this panel has the five reads. The third option is recommended: its 3 commands use the tool and the login that the UPDATE of D-AUTH-05 already uses, and each result shows 0 rows written. It is wrong if no agent may use that login for more than the two writes.

options.label: Nobody reads the live service
options.explanation: The implementation uses the code and the documents only. The five facts stay assumptions.
options.consequences: No work, and no use of your login for a read. It changes two of your answers. D-LOAD-02 says that the region comes from one D1 result: without it, the placement key waits, or it uses the assumption 'eastern North America', and a wrong region makes each request of each reviewer slower. D-CODE-02 says that the request count of the comparison Worker is read first: without it, the Worker is deleted on the evidence of the code alone. About 900 lines that read old data forms stay. Or they go on an assumption, and the page of an old run can fail. Both are against your rules 2 and 3. Nobody learns if an earlier database with stored sign-in tokens still exists. To reverse it, select another option later: Cloudflare keeps a trace for 7 days and the request count of a Worker for 3 months.

options.label: You make each read
options.explanation: The record lists 3 commands and 2 pages of the Cloudflare dashboard. You run them and put the results in the issue that needs them. No agent uses your Cloudflare login for a read.
options.consequences: About 15 minutes of your time (an estimate, not measured). Rows written: 0. The implementation waits for you at three places: the placement key of D-LOAD-02, the removal of the old readers, and the last step of D-CODE-02. Risk: a value that is copied wrongly, with no second look. Each of your answers and rules holds. Nothing to reverse.

options.label: The implementation runs the commands
options.explanation: The implementation runs 3 wrangler commands from a fixed list: the place of the database, 5 row counts, and the list of the databases of the account. It writes each result in the issue that uses it. You look at one number in the Cloudflare dashboard: the request count of the Worker visonaut-compare, because your answer to D-CODE-02 says 'read first'. The CPU time of one run page is a second look, if you want it.
options.consequences: About 1 minute of your time (an estimate), as a check box in the issue that deletes the Worker. Only that last step of D-CODE-02 waits for it. Rows written: 0, and the implementation checks it, because each result has the fields rows_written and changed_db. Rows read: each row of 5 small tables, in a database of 5.5 MiB. Risk: the login that reads can also write. So the list is fixed, each statement is a SELECT, and nothing else runs. Without the second look, nobody measures the gain of D-RUN-03 in production, and the look is possible only before that change is live. It fits rules 2 and 3: with a count of 0, an old reader goes with no data step. To leave out the first look also, write it in the notes: the record then changes the words 'read first' of D-CODE-02. To reverse it, stop: a read leaves nothing behind.

options.label: The implementation makes each read, also in the dashboard
options.explanation: The option before, and the implementation also opens the two pages of the Cloudflare dashboard in your Chrome session and reads the two numbers. The audit opened visonaut.com in that way on 2026-10-05.
options.consequences: No work for you, and each result is in the record. Rows written: 0. Risk: the dashboard session is your complete Cloudflare account: its billing, its DNS, and each project, also the ones that are not Visonaut. A wrong click there changes a setting, and a fixed list of commands cannot do that. The gain against the option before is about 1 minute of your time. To reverse it, close the tab.

settledAnswer: The implementation makes each of the five reads of the live service, and the maintainer makes none. A read is a look that changes nothing: no row, no check, and no pull request. Reads 1 to 3 are 3 wrangler commands from a fixed list: the place of the production database, 5 row counts, and the list of the databases of the account. Each statement is a SELECT, and nothing else runs. The implementation checks in each result that rows_written is 0 and that changed_db is false, and it writes each result in the issue that uses it. Reads 4 and 5 are two pages of the Cloudflare dashboard, which the implementation opens in the Chrome session of the maintainer: the CPU time of one run page in the traces of the Worker visonaut, and the request count of the Worker visonaut-compare. The implementation reads the two numbers there, and each result is in the record. It reads the request count before the last step of D-CODE-02 deletes the Worker, and it reads the CPU time before the change of D-RUN-03 is live.
rationale: The maintainer selected it in round 6 with no note. The recommended option was "The implementation runs the commands": the implementation runs the 3 commands, and the maintainer reads the request count in the dashboard, which is about 1 minute of his time (estimate). The selected option costs more in one point. The dashboard session is the complete Cloudflare account of the maintainer: its billing, its DNS, and each project, also the ones that are not Visonaut. A wrong click there changes a setting, and a fixed list of commands cannot do that. What it gives: no work for the maintainer, each result in the record, and the look at the CPU time, which the recommended option had only on request. So the gain of D-RUN-03 is measured in production: the server wait of a run page was 5.3 to 5.7 s on 2026-10-05 (measured). The evidence: the audit made no read, so five facts of the record are assumptions. Each of the 3 commands writes 0 rows, and the 5 counts read each row of 5 small tables in a database of 5.5 MiB (measured on 2026-10-05). The 5 statements ran against the 33 migrations in a local SQLite file, and not against D1 (measured). What the results decide: the region of the placement key of D-LOAD-02, which the record assumes as eastern North America. With a count of 0, an old reader goes with no data step: about 900 lines (estimate: 482 counted in two files, and about 420 from two findings). With a count above 0, the implementation looks at those rows first, and that code stays until the maintainer decides. If an earlier database still exists, it can hold stored sign-in tokens, and its end is a new question for the maintainer, because the UPDATE of D-AUTH-05 reaches only the database of today. A request count above 0 stops the deletion of the comparison Worker until the caller is known. It changes no earlier answer: D-LOAD-02 gets its one D1 result, and the words "read first" of D-CODE-02 hold. It changes no contract line: contract line 63 lists what needs a separate instruction, and a read is not in that list (counted). What the implementation does first: it tests that the wrangler login of the computer is valid and that it is for the account of Visonaut. A login file from 2026-10-05 exists (measured), and nobody tested it. It uses --command for the counts and not --file, because wrangler 4.136.1 imports a file into a remote database (counted from code). In the dashboard it opens only the two pages, and it changes no setting. The place of the traces in the dashboard is an assumption, and so are the 3 months for which Cloudflare keeps the request count. Cloudflare keeps a trace for 7 days (Cloudflare documentation). In the issue plan, the placement key (one step of the issue tooling) and steps 2 and 3 of the issue compare-worker waited for this answer. Two things are not in this decision, and the maintainer wrote no note about them: the one page load before and after the placement key (D-LOAD-02), and the look at two settings of the GitHub App (D-AUTH-02). By the text of the record, both stay with the maintainer. To reverse it, close the tab: a read leaves nothing behind.

question: Where must the production Worker run relative to D1?
context: In the model, placement alone moves the run list from 1,190 to 707 ms. After the round-trip fixes it adds only 80 ms and makes each document about 0.12 s later; the gain is then on the run page and on each saved decision. The region hint is recommended before Smart Placement because Cloudflare recommends hints for a Worker with one database, Smart Placement needs traffic from several locations, and the repository records that the same hint worked on this account. The region of the production database is not read, and no gain is measured.

options.label: No placement (today)
options.explanation: The Worker runs at the edge of the visitor. Only the number of round trips decreases, through D-LOAD-01 and D-LOAD-03.
options.consequences: Cost: none. Contract: no change. After the fixes, a dashboard read keeps 3 long round trips in sequence, about 0.4 s. The run page and each decision keep more of them. The document stays at 41 to 119 ms. A maintainer near the D1 primary sees no difference between the options.

options.label: A region hint near the D1 primary
options.explanation: Read the region of the database from one D1 result (meta.served_by_region). Then set "placement": { "region": "..." } in env.production, and measure one request before and after.
options.consequences: Cost: one configuration key and two measurements. Contract: no rule changes; line 188 says that no hosted diagnostic run is authorized, so you must authorize the measurement. Each Worker request from Brazil pays one long round trip to the Worker: the document, and with it the first paint of each page, is about 0.12 s later (assumption). A wrong region makes each request slower. The location is the same for all users. The queue consumer and the cron handler do not move. Reversible: remove the key.

options.label: Smart Placement
options.explanation: Set "placement": { "mode": "smart" }. Cloudflare selects the location from measured request times.
options.consequences: Cost: one configuration key. Contract: no change. No region to read. Cloudflare can leave the Worker at the edge with the status INSUFFICIENT_INVOCATIONS, because the service has a few users in a few locations. 1% of the requests stay at the edge as a baseline. When it moves the Worker, the document is later as in the option before. Reversible: remove the key.

settledAnswer: The production Worker gets a region hint near the D1 primary. The region comes from one D1 result (meta.served_by_region), and one /api/runs request is measured before and after the change.
rationale: Cloudflare recommends a hint for a Worker with one database, and Smart Placement needs traffic from several locations. In the model, placement alone moves the run list from 1,190 to 707 ms, and after the round-trip fixes the gain is on the run page (10 to 15 round trips) and on each saved decision (11 to 21). The answer is wrong if the D1 primary is not in eastern North America, or if a round trip from the placed Worker is not much shorter than 105 ms.

question: How must each private request pay for the access check?
context: Lines 186 and 204 of the contract require live session and linked-account reads for each request, and permit a positive permission result for 60 s on reads and 10 s on Approve and Reject. The second option is recommended because a local D1 run gave 2 round trips for the check where today has 5 (2 of the 5 are the schema check), with no contract change; nobody tested it in the Workers runtime. The gain of the third option is not known, because no trace shows how often a request reaches a new isolate.

options.label: Keep the reads and the caches of today
options.explanation: Only the schema check goes (D-LOAD-01). Session, user, linked account, and project stay separate round trips.
options.consequences: Cost: none. Contract: no change. The check stays 3 round trips on /api/runs and 4 on other requests. The first Approve of a visit keeps 2 live GitHub checks in sequence. A new isolate keeps 3 GitHub calls, 0.7 to 1.0 s (estimate).

options.label: Batch the reads; a write check keeps the grant
options.explanation: Set joins: true so that the session statement returns the user. Read the project at the same time. Store the positive result of each live check, also of a write check. A write still never reads the grant.
options.consequences: Cost: S to M. The check is 2 round trips in sequence. The first Approve makes 1 live check. Contract: no change; lines 19 and 26 of packages/security/README.md change, because a write check becomes a source of the grant. What can go wrong: joins changes the SQL of each Better Auth read that has a join, also in the OAuth callback, so one sign-in on the deployed service is necessary. An anonymous request to a deployment with a wrong project gets 401, not 503. Reversible: one option and a few lines.

options.label: Also store the login hint, or the grant, in D1
options.explanation: The option before, plus stored state that each isolate reads in the statement for the linked account. Step 1: the login hint. Step 2: the grant, with the limits of 60 s and 10 s from the start of the GitHub request.
options.consequences: Cost: M for the grant; the login hint alone is a smaller change. With the hint, a new isolate makes 2 GitHub calls, not 3, with no new write and no access state. A verifier found that the hint gives almost all of the gain: a stored grant removes the other calls only when another isolate made a check less than 60 s before, and it adds one D1 write for each live check (today one each minute for each open dashboard tab). The recovery procedure must delete the new table. Contract: no text changes; a stored grant is a new decision about access state at rest. The installation token is not stored: it can write checks. Reversible: drop the table.

options.label: A signed access grant in a cookie
options.explanation: The Worker signs the session, the linked account, and the permission into a cookie with a short lifetime. While the cookie is valid, a request makes no D1 read and no GitHub call for access.
options.consequences: Cost: the audit has no estimate. The check is 0 round trips. Contract: this reopens line 186 (“Live session and linked-account checks still run for every request”), the recorded decisions O05 and O08 (read permission for at most 60 seconds), and the decision of 2026-10-02 (10 seconds for Approve and Reject). A session that signed out and a maintainer who lost access both keep access for the lifetime of the cookie. A failed live check cannot delete a cookie that a browser holds. Hard to reverse after the contract changes.

settledAnswer: The access check reads the session and the user in one statement (joins: true), reads the project at the same time, and stores the positive result of each live GitHub check, also of a write check. A write still never reads the stored result.
rationale: A local D1 run gave 2 round trips for the check where today has 5, with no contract change. The first Approve of a visit then makes 1 live GitHub check in place of 2. Nobody tested it in the Workers runtime, and one sign-in on the deployed service is necessary, because joins changes the SQL of Better Auth.

question: Where must the first run list come from?
context: The request starts 199 to 303 ms after the first byte of the document. After the other fixes, the model has that gap at 28 to 31% of the time to the list. The head request is recommended, and not the server loader that 5 audit lanes recommended first: 3 second verifiers found that the head request removes the same gap with the same endpoint, and that a read in the document request is a second path to private data with 5 rules of its own. D-UX-02 in the section UI structure decides the routes; the script and the read follow the route.

options.label: After hydration (today)
options.explanation: The document has the loading text. The request starts in an effect when the JavaScript is ready.
options.consequences: Cost: none. Contract: no change. The run list stays 0.2 to 0.3 s later on a fast machine, and about 2 s later in the one guest load with slow 4G and a 4 times slower CPU.

options.label: Start the request in the document head
options.explanation: An inline script with the nonce starts fetch("/api/runs") while the JavaScript files load. The page uses that promise one time.
options.consequences: Cost: one inline script and a change of the first read. Gain: the 0.2 to 0.3 s (estimate; not built). Contract: no change; the endpoint, the access check, and the response rules are the same. What can go wrong: the page must take the promise exactly one time and must fetch again on Refresh and after a router navigation; the URL of the read is then in 2 places. With the route loader of D-LOAD-05, the loader takes the promise. Reversible: remove the script.

options.label: Read in the document request, streamed
options.explanation: A route loader starts the access check and the read when the Worker gets the document request, and returns a promise. The document streams the shell first and the list after it.
options.consequences: Cost: M. Gain: the 0.2 to 0.3 s and one request less (13 to 90 ms more than the head request in the model). Contract: the access rules do not change, but the document then has private data and the read must repeat 5 rules of the API path (table above). This extends the recorded decision P03, whose note says that server loading “would need a separately scoped authenticated server read”. What can go wrong: a loader that awaits moves 0.9 to 2.0 s in front of the first byte today. Reversible with more work: it adds a second read path.

settledAnswer: The first run list comes from a route loader that starts on the server in the document request. The loader returns a promise, so the document streams the page shell first and the list after it.
rationale: The maintainer selected it in place of the recommended head request, with the note that it looks like the idiomatic way and that the inline script looks like a hack. The TanStack Start documentation agrees: a route loader with a streamed document is the documented way. It removes the gap of 199 to 303 ms and one request at effort M, and it must return its promise without await, use the access check of the API path, and leave the session renewal to a later request.

question: What must a return to the dashboard show while the new run list loads?
context: Each mount starts with the loading text and reads the list again. The router defaults are recommended because they show the last list at once with no new dependency, as the recorded decision P03 selected for the run page (“Use the existing router loaders”). D-UX-05 in the section UI structure decides how the list stays current while the page is open; this decision is only about a new mount.

options.label: Component state (today)
options.explanation: The list lives in the dashboard component. Each mount starts with the loading text.
options.consequences: Cost: none. Contract: no change. Each return from a run shows the loading text for the time of /api/runs: 0.9 to 2.0 s today, about 0.4 s after the fixes of D-LOAD-01 and D-LOAD-03 (estimate). No row is wrong at any time. The browser keeps no private list after the page changes.

options.label: A route loader with the router defaults
options.explanation: The dashboard read moves to a route loader in the browser, as on the run route. A return shows the last list at once and reads again in the background.
options.consequences: Cost: M. It works for browser Back at once; the Queue button of the run page stays a document load until it is a router link. Contract: no server change. The browser keeps the private list in memory for 5 minutes after the reviewer leaves the dashboard; today the list is in the page while the tab is open. A fresh time (staleTime) above 0 is not part of this option: 2 verifiers found that it shows a wrong row for up to that time. What can go wrong: a row can be wrong for the time of one request after a decision; a background read that gets 401 or 403 must replace the list at once; sign-out must clear the cache. Reversible: remove the loader.

options.label: A query cache library
options.explanation: A client library keeps the list, shows it at once, and reads again in the background, on window focus, and on an interval.
options.consequences: Cost: more than the loader, and one new dependency; the audit has no estimate. It also gives the refresh on focus and on an interval that D-UX-05 asks about. Recorded decisions: this reopens P03, where the option “Add a query cache layer” was not selected (“no measured need in this three-page app”). Line 53 of the contract records “No new workflow framework or global store” for the workspace refactor (D08 and D09). An earlier audit note says that permission caching “must not acquire an additional unbounded client-cache lifetime”, so the cache needs a time limit. Reversible with more work.

settledAnswer: The dashboard read is a route loader with the router defaults and no fresh time (staleTime) above 0: a return to the dashboard shows the last list at once and reads again in the background. It is the same loader as the one of D-LOAD-04.
rationale: It needs no new dependency, and it is the pattern of the run page, which the earlier decision P03 ('Use the existing router loaders') selected. In a small browser build with the installed router, the last list stayed on screen while the loader read again, where today each return shows the loading text. The browser keeps the private list in memory for 5 minutes after the reviewer leaves the dashboard, so a sign-out must clear it and a 401 or 403 must replace it at once.

question: What does the first response of a run page contain?
context: Today one response has a record for each variant, and the server reads 24.3 MB from R2 to build it. P01 selected this complete model. Its record says what opens it again: "A route measurement shows that complete-model reads or parse time exceed the selected budget after compression and simple query cleanup". The measurement exists now; a budget and the cleanup do not. Reason for the recommendation: the cost of the complete model follows the size of the test suite (measured at 1, 2, and 3 times the count of today, which grew from 1,058 to 3,832 in about 10 days), and the cost of the attention-first response follows the size of the change (7.5 KB, measured). Against it: it is the largest change of this section, and its time gain is an estimate. A complete model that meets a budget that you set, after the no-regret list and D-RUN-03, invalidates the recommendation.

options.label: Keep one complete model
options.explanation: One response with a record for each variant, as P01 selected. Remove the repeated fields (the image URL that repeats the image ID, the label that repeats its parts, the long ID prefix), and send the two digests of the rendering profiles only for the rows that D1 stores.
options.consequences: Measured on the fixture: the repeated fields are 19% of the JSON and 5% of the transfer, and the digests are 25% of the JSON and 24% of the transfer. The server wait does not change: with the no-regret list, D-RUN-03, and both R2 reads together, the model of this section gives 4.2 to 4.5 s to the workspace (estimate). The cost grows with the test suite. P01 and line 26 of the contract stay. The Details panel loses the digest line for an unchanged variant. The API and the page change together, and an open tab with the old page needs a reload.

options.label: Attention-first response
options.explanation: The first response has the run header, the counts, and the rows that D1 stores: changed, added, and removed captures. The unchanged variants load in a second request when the reviewer opens Accepted, searches, or follows a link to one of them.
options.consequences: Measured on the fixture: 7.5 KB in place of 5.33 MB, and no R2 read. Estimate: 3.9 to 4.5 s less server wait for each first load. Reopens P01. Line 26 of the contract ("Review reads the full inventory to show unchanged items") becomes a later read. Submit must store the baseline image, the name, and the variant with each changed or removed row, in a new column of D1; older runs need the read of today as a fallback. The page needs new rules: a merge of two responses with different revisions, a loading state for the list, a link to an unchanged variant (U06), the screenshot count of Accepted, and Approve before the check that each changed capture has a stored row. A run with no change shows no review area at first (D-WORK-05). Effort L. Reversible while the complete response stays available.

options.label: Paged model
options.explanation: The response has one page of screenshots in list order. More pages load when the list scrolls.
options.consequences: No part of the audit measured it. The search, the counts, and the keyboard order use all screenshots today, so each needs a new rule. With one inventory object, each page reads the same 24.3 MB again, so it needs the paged inventory of D-DATA-02 or the review index of D-RUN-03 first. Reopens P01. Effort L.

settledAnswer: The first response of a run has the run header, the counts, and the rows that D1 stores: changed, added, and removed captures. The unchanged variants load in a second request when the reviewer opens Accepted, searches, or follows a link to one of them.
rationale: On the fixture the response is 7.5 KB in place of 5.33 MB with no R2 read, and the estimate is 3.9 to 4.5 s less server wait for each first load. Its cost follows the size of the change, not the size of the test suite, which grew from 1,058 to 3,832 captures in about 10 days. It reopens the earlier decision P01 ('One compact complete model') and changes contract line 26, and Submit must store the baseline image, the name, and the variant of each changed or removed row in a new D1 column, which adds no written row when the column is on a row that Submit already writes (local measurement).

question: How does the server get the complete capture list for a review read?
context: Each model read downloads two inventories and validates them again. Submit validated them when it wrote them, and the object key has the digest. Reason for the recommendation: the digest-only read is the only option with a measured gain for a first load (680 to 225 ms in local workerd, the same response bytes), it adds no stored object, and no line of the contract asks for validation on each read. It changes a tested trust rule, so it needs your decision. The production gain is an estimate until someone reads a trace: a CPU time near 0.7 s in the trace invalidates the recommendation, because the gain is then about 0.5 s. With the recommended options of D-RUN-02 and D-RUN-05, this read is no longer in the first response or in a saved decision: it stays for the unchanged list, for the runs of today, and for Submit. The format of the inventory is D-DATA-02 in the data section.

options.label: Validate on each read
options.explanation: No change. Each review read downloads both inventories, checks the size and the digest, and runs the complete validation again.
options.consequences: Each read applies the validation rules of today, also to an object that an older version wrote. The cost stays for each page load and each ready decision receipt: 24.3 MB from R2, and 0.60 to 0.70 s of CPU on a laptop (1.3 to 2.3 s in production, estimate). Both grow in a straight line with the capture count.

options.label: Check the digest only
options.explanation: A review read keeps the key, size, and digest checks. It skips the canonical check, the manifest schema, the digests of the rendering profiles, and the check of the comparison result. Submit, promotion, and recovery keep the complete validation.
options.consequences: Measured in local workerd: 680 to 225 ms for the first request of a new isolate, with the same response bytes. Estimate for production: 1.0 to 1.8 s less. question: How does a /pulls link of a GitHub check reach the review?

options.label: Keep the lookup in the page
options.explanation: No change of the flow. The no-regret list loads the code of the run route while the lookup runs.
options.consequences: The extra request stays on three paths: a check that still waits for captures, the short time between a ready run and the status delivery, and an old link. options.label: Redirect in the Worker
options.explanation: For a /pulls link, the Worker reads the session, finds the run, and answers with a redirect to /runs/<id> when the run is ready. In each other case it renders the page of today.
options.consequences: The same 8 round trips run before the first byte, so the tab stays blank where the loading card is today. A document request replaces the API request: no round trip goes away. question: What does the server return when it has saved a queued decision?
context: Today each ready decision receipt and each Undo build the complete review model again: 25 round trips, 2 R2 reads of 24.3 MB, and 5.33 MB of JSON for one decision. Against it: the model in each decision receipt needs no merge rule, and it costs less when D-RUN-02 makes the model small.

options.explanation: No change. Each ready decision receipt and each Undo return a new review model from the server.
options.consequences: The page is correct after each decision with no merge rule, also when a second reviewer decides at the same time. Each decision costs what a page load costs, so the cost follows D-RUN-02 and D-RUN-03. With the complete model of today, decisions that are faster than one model build keep the earlier ones unconfirmed until the reviewer stops. options.explanation: The decision receipt carries the rows that changed since the last read of the page, built from D1 only. The page merges them into its model.
options.consequences: The server stays the source of each changed row, also for the decisions of another reviewer. No R2 read. The page needs a merge rule that does not exist today, and no part of the audit built or measured this option. Effort M to L.

settledAnswer: A clean save returns the stored decision receipt and the current run revision, with no model, and the page reads the model again only when the run revision is not the one that it expects. A conflict, a failed decision, and Undo keep the model.
rationale: Measured on a fixture: 9 round trips in place of 25, no R2 read, and 425 bytes in place of 5.33 MB. question: Does the service keep the GitHub user token of each sign-in?

question: Does sign-in stay on the GitHub App that writes the check, or move to a separate App with no repository permission?
context: GitHub App 5028451 signs users in and holds checks: write, so the sign-in token of a maintainer can, by the GitHub documentation, write the required check. Nobody tested this with a real token. One App is recommended on one condition: the routes are closed (D-AUTH-01) and no token is stored (D-AUTH-05). The token then exists only in Worker memory during the sign-in callback, and the Worker already holds the private key of the App, which can write the same check. If one of the two stays open, the separate App is the only change that takes the permission from the token.

options.label: Keep one App
options.explanation: Sign-in stays on App 5028451. The operations README records its three required settings: private, token expiry on, device flow off.
options.consequences: No setup and no new secret. The contract sentence "Keep installation tokens separate from Better Auth user login tokens" holds for the code paths and for storage, not for the App identity. What can go wrong: a later change opens a route or stores the token again, or someone enables device flow, and the token can write the check again with no warning. Nothing to reverse.

options.explanation: A second private GitHub App with no repository permission gives its client ID and secret to Better Auth. App 5028451 keeps the installation, the checks, and the CI webhooks.
options.consequences: A sign-in token can never write a check, also after a later regression. Cost: one more App registration with its own private setting, and a second webhook URL and secret for the revocation event. Device flow must stay off on App 5028451 in this option too. An OAuth App is not a safe substitute: the GitHub documentation names no private setting for it, so sign-in can open to each GitHub account (not tested). To reverse, set the old client ID again.

settledAnswer: Sign-in stays on GitHub App 5028451. The operations README records its three required settings: private, token expiry on, device flow off.
rationale: With the routes closed (D-AUTH-01) and no token stored (D-AUTH-05), the sign-in token exists only in Worker memory during the callback, and the Worker already holds the private key of the App, which can write the same check. question: What does an open review page do when its sign-in ends or is replaced?
context: Today the first sign is a failed save. After a new sign-in, a tab that already saved a decision cannot save until a reload, and a 401 names no way to sign in. options.explanation: On review_session_expired the client starts a new review session and sends the same command again. On a 401 the bar keeps the held decisions, also after a refresh that fails, and shows a "Sign in again" link that opens a new tab.
options.consequences: Small, client only, no contract change. It needs error.code in the client, which is in the list of D-RES-01. options.consequences: Small to medium, client only. No private text stays on screen after a sign-out. A decision that was not sent is lost. After sign-in the run loads again at the same screenshot and variant: 6.7 to 7.8 s for a large run today.

question: What does the service do when pull request code loosens the comparison settings?

The server cannot change an outcome, so the CLI must apply the rule: a protocol field, a CLI release, a new workflow pin in Ariakit, and a service pin update. short: Cause of a failed pass in the log
question: When a background pass fails, the log will say where it failed. May the log also say why?
context: Each 5 minutes, and after each event, the service runs a background pass: it sends check results to GitHub, promotes baselines, and deletes old images. A pass writes to the log of the Cloudflare Worker. That log is not public: only a person with access to the Cloudflare account of the service reads it (an assumption: the audit did not read the account). Today each place that catches an error in a pass drops the error. You accepted row 7 of the fix list of D-OPS-01: one log line for each pass, with the step that failed and the time and the counts of each step. Row 7 left the cause to you, because the contract has this rule for a failure line (line 81): fixed fields, and no "raw exception". Example: GitHub answers 502 when the pass sends a check result. With row 7 alone, the line says that 1 item of the step "checks" failed. Nothing says that GitHub was the cause. No option adds a D1 write.

options.label: 1. Where only: the fields of row 7, and no cause
options.explanation: Nothing more than you accepted. The line names the step that failed, and it gives the time and the counts of each step.
options.consequences: Cost: none above row 7. The line says where a pass failed and how many items failed. It does not say why. To learn the cause, the operator makes the failure occur again or reads D1 by hand. For a failed check result D1 holds the error text (the column work_status_outbox.last_error). For a GitHub failure that text is one fixed sentence with no status number. For each other step nothing holds the cause. Standing rules: no D1 write (rule 1) and the least code (rule 3). To reverse: add fields later in one service deployment.

options.label: 2. Add three fixed values: error name, error code, and GitHub status
options.explanation: Each place that catches an error in a pass can log three values of it: the name of the error class (for example SecurityError or ConflictError), the fixed code of a SecurityError (for example github_unavailable), and the HTTP status number that GitHub answered. Each value is on a list in the source code. A name that is not on the list becomes "other". The log never gets a message text or a stack.
options.consequences: Cost: about 20 lines and their tests (estimate), in the same change as row 7. The example becomes: step checks, errorName SecurityError, code github_unavailable, upstreamStatus 502. A request to GitHub that got no answer shows as the same code with no status. Limit: a D1 failure shows only as the name "Error". From code reading, most failures that stop a whole step are D1 failures, because each step catches the GitHub failures of its items. Risk: low. No value comes from a request, a manifest, or a database row. Contract: the rule of line 81 stays. Standing rules: no D1 write (rule 1) and no data of a customer in the log (rule 5). To reverse: delete the fields.

Example of the form of a D1 message, not a recorded line: "D1_ERROR: UNIQUE constraint failed: work_checks.id". Risk: a message is free text. Each value is on a list in the source code, and a name that is not on the list becomes "other". The log never gets a message text or a stack. No D1 write is added.

short: A Reject that does not stay
question: When a reviewer rejects a carried approval, which decision counts for later runs with the same pixels?
context: Measured: after an approval in run 1 and a Reject of its copy in run 2, run 3 is approved again by a new copy, and after the merge the main run takes the pixels into the baseline. C02 selected "copy" and names only the other direction, so this direction is undecided. The second option is marked as recommended for four reasons: the code is not consistent with itself today, the code before C02 refused such a copy, the changed rule is measured, and it writes no closed history.

options.label: Keep the copy rule
options.explanation: A Reject applies to its own run. A later run copies the oldest valid approval of the same pixels again. The review guide gets one sentence that says so.
options.consequences: No code change, and C02 stays as written. The required check can be success after the newest human verdict was Reject: a push, a workflow re-run, or the merge is sufficient. For a screenshot that is new in the pull request, the baseline can change with 0 human approvals. The code owner approval after the last push is then the one barrier.

options.label: The newest decision for the same pixels wins
options.explanation: The service makes no new copy when the lineage has a current Reject of the same tuple that is newer than the approval. A newer first-hand approval makes copies possible again.
options.consequences: One more condition in the reuse rule, with the two digest predicates of the second check: 10,225 rows read in the test, against 10,125 today. It runs only when a comparison becomes ready. It revokes no copy, so the C02 sentence of the contract stays true, and it does not write closed history (D05). It adds back one cross-run effect of the kind that C02 removed. The time order uses clock values of different Worker invocations. To reverse it, remove the condition.

options.label: A Reject also revokes the source approval
options.explanation: When a reviewer rejects a copy, the service also revokes the decision that the copy came from.
options.consequences: The Reject then holds for every later run, until a new first-hand approval. The source is in a closed run, so this reopens D05 (all closed history is read-only) and the C02 rule that a later change does not cross runs. A revoked source stays revoked when the code is removed.

settledAnswer: The service makes no new copy of an approval when the lineage has a current Reject of the same pixels that is newer than the approval. A newer first-hand approval makes copies possible again.
rationale: Measured: after an approval in run 1 and a Reject of its copy in run 2, run 3 is approved again by a new copy, and after the merge the rejected pixels become the baseline. The new rule is one more condition (10,225 rows read against 10,125 in the test) and no write. It revokes no copy and writes no closed history, and the earlier decision C02 ('Copy verified approval into each new run') named only the other direction.

question: Which conclusion does the check have on GitHub while a review waits for a maintainer?
context: Today it is failure, the same as for a Reject and for a failed run. D20 requires that the check blocks the merge, not that it is red. GitHub passes a required check for neutral, so neutral is not an option: the pull request could merge. "Keep failure" is marked as recommended because it has no open question: action_required is not tested on GitHub and needs a D1 table rebuild, and in_progress becomes stale after 14 days. One test of action_required on a test repository can change this.

options.label: Keep failure
options.explanation: The check stays completed with the conclusion failure. A title for each state is a separate choice (decision D-OPS-07).
options.consequences: No schema change. The check blocks the merge: the branch rules of Ariakit require it, and the GitHub documentation passes only success, skipped, and neutral. A review that waits stays red on the pull request and on a main commit.

options.label: Use action_required
options.explanation: The check is completed with the conclusion action_required while changes wait for a decision. A Reject and a failed run stay failure.
options.consequences: The GitHub documentation does not list it as successful, so it blocks a required check. How GitHub shows it on a pull request is not verified. Cost: the conclusion column allows 3 values, so D1 needs a table rebuild; the types, 6 code sites that read a remote conclusion, and a second copy of the mapping must change.

options.label: Use in_progress
options.explanation: The check stays in progress until a maintainer decides. The code does this for merge queue runs today.
options.consequences: Yellow, not red, and it blocks the merge. GitHub sets the conclusion stale when a check run is incomplete for more than 14 days, so a pull request that waits longer gets a stale check. The same status then means capture, comparison, and waiting for a person.

settledAnswer: The check stays completed with the conclusion failure while a review waits for a maintainer.
rationale: It blocks the merge with no open question and no schema change. action_required is not tested on GitHub and needs a D1 table rebuild, in_progress becomes stale after 14 days, and neutral lets the pull request merge. The title and the counts of D-OPS-07 say which of the three failure states the run has.

question: What does the public check output contain?
context: D25 selected a generic status and a sign-in link. Today one title covers three states, and one sentence tells every reader to sign in. The second option is marked as recommended because it removes the measured confusion and adds no number and no name to a public check.

question: What does a decision do when another write of the project commits at the same time?
context: Each decision asserts one project revision, and each write that can change a check moves it. Measured locally: one reviewer lost 0 of 60 decisions, and two reviewers who started in the same instant lost 17 of 40. "Keep" is marked as recommended while one person reviews at a time: no wrong state is saved, and the estimate for a lost decision is 1 in 2,450 or less. The lane auditor recommended the retry. Two persons who review at the same time make the retry the better option.

options.label: Keep one version for the project
options.explanation: A decision that loses the race answers 409 with the current state, and the reviewer decides again. The message says that another change was saved at the same time.
options.consequences: No change to the write path that must never publish a wrong success. Estimate for a lost decision: 1 in 2,450 to 1 in 68,600 from CI events; 0.25% to 7% while a second reviewer saves one decision each 2 seconds. The queued decisions behind a lost one are also not saved, as the contract rule for a failed predecessor requires.

options.label: Retry on the server
options.explanation: When the write batch fails and the command was not saved, the service reads again and tries again, 3 times at most.
options.consequences: Measured: the second attempt costs 3 more D1 calls and saves the decision, and a row that is really stale gives the exact error with the row. No contract change. Risks: the retry depends on a pattern match of the D1 error text, Undo needs the same loop with 7 calls for each attempt, and the loop needs a fixed end.

options.label: A version for each run
options.explanation: Approve, Reject, and Undo assert the row revisions, the comparison state, and the promotion state. They do not assert the project revision or the run revision.
options.consequences: Removes the cause, also between pull requests. It changes the guards of the path that publishes success: four stored values must then come from SQL in the same batch, and the race tests of the saved contract are necessary. The largest change of the three.

settledAnswer: A decision that loses the race with another write of the project answers 409 with the current state, and the reviewer decides again. The message says that another change was saved at the same time.
rationale: One reviewer lost 0 of 60 decisions in the local test, and no wrong state is saved. The estimate for a lost decision is 1 in 2,450 or less while one person reviews at a time. Two persons who review at the same time lost 17 of 40 decisions when they started in the same instant: that case makes the retry on the server the better option.

question: How does a run of the consumer repository prove to the service that it may submit captures?
context: Today the proof has two parts. The OIDC token of GitHub Actions says who calls. Two exact file hashes, of ci.yml and of app.yml, say which code ran. All of the cost comes from the file hashes: each edit of the 451 lines is a pin cutover of two repositories, with 34 to 41 minutes in which the runs of other pull requests fail (4 measured cases). Your note asks if API keys are simpler. A key replaces only the first part, and it makes the second part impossible. The options are in the order of work for the consumer, from the least to the most. No option adds a D1 write for a request, and no option gives a pull request from a fork a Visonaut check.

options.label: 1. Keep the OIDC token, and check no workflow file
options.explanation: The proof is the OIDC token alone. GitHub signs the repository, the commit, the run, and the job, and the service checks them as today. It compares no file hash. It also stops the comparison of a third pinned value, the package digest of the capture adapter: app.yml declares that digest, and a pull request can then edit app.yml, so the comparison proves nothing. Lines 157 to 206 of oidc.ts, the three pinned values, the repository variable, and the pin runbook go away. The consumer needs no secret and no API key. This was option 1 of revision r2, and the option "Trust repository and successful jobs only" of the earlier decision A02.
options.consequences: Consumer: delete one line, then nothing for each kind of workflow edit, also for an update of Renovate, and nothing but a version change for a release of the CLI or of the capture adapter. No secret to create, to store, or to replace. A new customer later needs 2 steps: install the GitHub App and add the workflow lines. The signed repository number binds each run to one project, with no key table. Gives up: a pull request of an account with push access can replace the Submit job, and then code of the pull request counts the changed pixels. It can also send the no-visual report for itself. What is left: the workflow edit is in the diff of that pull request, and the branch rule of ariakit/ariakit asks for 1 approval. The same 5 accounts can already pass false screenshots through the capture code (TRUST-03). The count of loose settings of D-AUTH-04 is then true only in a run that did not replace the Submit job. Does not work outside GitHub Actions: API keys can be added later as a second proof. The least to build: it deletes code in both repositories and needs one CLI release and at most one last pin cutover. Changes the earlier decisions A02 and D39 (a pinned file of Ariakit holds the list of the required capture jobs) and contract lines 218 to 230.

options.label: 2. Keep the OIDC token, and move the Submit job to a workflow file of the service repository
options.explanation: The Submit job becomes a reusable workflow in ariakit/visonaut, and app.yml calls it with one "uses" line. The service accepts a Submit only when the OIDC claim job_workflow_ref names that file on the branch main of ariakit/visonaut. The service accepts the no-visual report of the Plan job when ci.yml of the pull request is the same file as on main. No consumer file has a pin, and the consumer needs no secret.
options.consequences: Consumer: one refactor and one rule of 4 lines in renovate.json. The Submit job goes from 44 lines to 8, and the repository variable goes away. After that, no workflow edit and no update of Renovate needs a service change, and no failure window exists. Keeps what options 1 and 3 give up: a pull request cannot replace the Submit job, and it cannot send the no-visual report for itself. 2 accounts can change the Submit file in ariakit/visonaut. 5 accounts can push to ariakit/ariakit. Gives up: the service no longer checks the text of the capture steps and of the other CI jobs. Those steps already run pull request code (TRUST-03). A later customer calls the same file, so its capture jobs need the job names and the artifact names that the file expects. Cost for the service: the new workflow file, one CLI release, changes in the 7 files that compare a pin, and one last pin cutover. The package digest line of app.yml (PIPE-05) moves to the service file or goes away. Changes the earlier decisions A02 and D39 (the service file then holds the list of the required capture jobs) and contract lines 218 to 230. Not verified in these two repositories: one run before the cutover must confirm the claim for the branch main.

options.label: 3. Replace the OIDC token with an API key
options.explanation: A repository administrator creates a key on a settings page of the service. The page shows it one time. The consumer stores it as the repository secret VISONAUT_API_KEY and gives it to the CLI in 2 env lines. The service stores only a hash of the key, in one new D1 table, with own code and no library. The OIDC token, the file check, and the comparison of the package digest of the capture adapter go away, as in option 1. The GitHub App stays: it writes the check and reads the run (D-AUTH-02).
options.consequences: Consumer: create the key, add 1 secret and 2 lines, remove 3 lines. Then nothing for each workflow edit. A person must replace the key when someone with access leaves or when the key was in a log. A new customer later needs 4 steps. Gives: the proof that users of other products know (all 6 compared CI products offer a key), and a proof that can work outside GitHub Actions. Visonaut cannot use the second today, because the Submit job reads the capture artifacts of the run from GitHub. Gives up the same as option 1: a pull request can replace the Submit job. Gives up more: the key is the same in each run and has no end date. A workflow edit in a pull request can read it, and a copied key works from another computer until someone revokes it, also for the run of another pull request. For ariakit/ariakit this risk is not new: the same 5 accounts can read its 9 repository secrets in the same way today. With own code, a key check is 1 D1 read and 0 writes (local probe). The API key plugin of Better Auth writes 2 rows for each check, so it breaks the rule about D1 writes. options.label: 4. Keep today: the OIDC token and one exact file hash for each of two files

question: Where does a run stop when the service is at its capacity limit, and what does the check say?
context: The capacity stop is deliberate. On 2026-10-04 it refused 5 Submit steps after the complete capture, and the check gave no reason. The database is now at 5.5 MiB of the 2,048 MiB limit, so a repeat of the size stop is far less probable. The first option is marked as recommended because it needs no CLI release, no cutover, and no contract change.

options.label: Keep the place, say the reason on the check
options.explanation: The stop stays in the reserve call of Submit. The refusal completes the check as failure with the capacity text. The stop at 5 active runs gets its own text and its own alert.
options.consequences: No contract change, no migration, no cutover. One more GitHub write in a request that fails. A refused run still uses the capture jobs first: 19 min 49 s to 23 min 32 s of runner time in the 4 measured runs.

options.label: Refuse at the first call of Submit
options.explanation: The call that creates the check also tests the capacity.
options.consequences: The refusal comes about 1 minute earlier: today the step refuses in second 50 to 67 (measured). The capture is already complete at that time. With CLI 0.5.4 the job log then prints "The signed Submit check could not be started." and loses the capacity sentence, until a CLI release and a pin cutover.

options.label: Refuse in the Plan job, before the capture
options.explanation: The Plan job asks the service before the capture jobs start, with a signed report or with a read of a public state.
options.consequences: A refused run stops after about 40 seconds and uses no capture runner. A signed report for app=true reverses contract line 224 ("There is no separate signed true report"). A public read publishes one bit of service state and adds a D1 read to an anonymous path. Both need a new step in ci.yml, so one cutover. A stop that starts after Plan still refuses at Submit.

options.label: Accept the run and wait
options.explanation: The CLI waits and sends the reserve call again for a limited time.
options.consequences: Helps only for the stop at 5 active runs. The size stop needs a person, so the job waits and then fails. Needs a CLI release and a cutover. The signed token is valid for 10 minutes, so the job must request a new one for each try.

settledAnswer: When the service is at its limit of 5 active runs, the CLI waits and sends the reserve call again for a limited time. The capacity check of the reserve call only reads, so a refused try writes no D1 row.
rationale: The maintainer selected the wait in place of the recommended text on the check: a refused run cost 19 min 49 s to 23 min 32 s of runner time in the 4 measured runs, and a wait keeps that capture. It needs a CLI release, and it does not help the size stop, which needs a person. Each refused try writes 3 rows today (local measurement), so a wait with 20 tries would write 60. The check that only reads writes 0 rows (measured on a local D1, not built in the service) and removes code, and the scheduled pass keeps the snapshot and the alert each 5 minutes. This form follows the rule of the maintainer that D1 writes that repeat must not increase. Revision r4: D-DATA-02 adds a refusal for a run above the capture limit. The CLI must not wait on that refusal, so it needs its own error code.

question: Do you accept the no-regret list of this section?
context: The list has 17 fixes: 15 small and 2 medium. Each has one correct behavior and changes no line of the contract, which is the reason for the recommendation. Three have a date or an effect that a person sees today: the retention tests, the size alert, and the titles.

options.label: Accept the list
options.explanation: All 17 fixes go to implementation. The retention tests are first.
options.consequences: Two new migration files, for the title table and the indexes. One fix needs a release of the capture adapter. options.label: Accept with exceptions
options.explanation: The list goes to implementation without the fixes that you name in the notes.

settledAnswer: The 17 fixes of the data list go to implementation, and the retention tests are first. Three fixes take a form with no D1 write: no new index (two query rewrites remove the two largest scans), the pull request title stays in the webhook payload in place of a title table, and the alert for a large inventory is a read of the size that the run row already holds.

The retention tests must be in the repository before the first image deletion on the new form, which is not before 2026-11-03. On a local D1 the six indexes of r1 added 1 written row to each decision and 5 to each run. The two query rewrites read 6,581 rows in place of 1,203,980, with the same result and 0 written rows. The title that stays in the payload writes the same 6 rows as today. These forms follow the rule of the maintainer that D1 writes that repeat must not increase. They were measured on synthetic data and are not built in the service. Revision r4: with the pages of rows of D-DATA-02, the size column of the run row names the page index. So the alert for a large inventory reads the capture count of the run row against the capture limit.

short: Inventory format and its size limit
question: What format does the run inventory have, so that the capture count of a run has no practical limit?
context: Your note selected pages for scale: 'We may have hundreds of thousands of screenshots in the future.' Pages are the right form. But the option of revision r2 kept the records of today: the CLI still stops a run at about 5,700 captures, and 100,000 captures are 320 MB. Pages of short rows reach the number: 100,000 captures are 50 objects of about 0.8 MB. No option adds a D1 write. The recommendation is a path with two steps, because the format and the CLI need a change in Ariakit and the rest does not.

options.label: Keep the format, refuse early
options.explanation: One object with the embedded manifest, as today. The no-regret list adds the alerts. The service also refuses a run that cannot fit when the CLI sends the manifest, before the uploads, with a reason that names the limit.
options.consequences: Your notes of both rounds reject this limit. The option stays as the one that changes no format. The stop stays at about 5,260 captures, 1,427 more than today, and at about 4,750 when every capture changed (measured with the real writer: 13.54 MB at 3,832 captures). A refused run needs a new Submit after a fix. No contract change and no D1 change. Reversible.

options.label: Pages of rows now, Submit page by page later
options.explanation: The CLI sends the captures as rows, 2,000 in each page, in the order of the item name and the variant name. The service stores pages of rows and one page index, and D1 points to the index. The review page reads the unchanged captures one page at a time. Submit validation, materialization, promotion, and the recovery check keep their code: they read the pages one after the other and get the complete list. The service refuses a run above about 20,000 captures with a clear reason. Later, when a suite comes near that number, these steps change to work on one page at a time. That later step changes no format, no CLI, and nothing in Ariakit.
options.consequences: Measured with a prototype: the 3,832 captures of today are 2 pages of 0.83 and 0.78 MB and an index of 913 bytes, in place of one object of 12.15 MB. It removes the stops at 5,260, 5,700, 9,150, and 10,600 captures. The limit of about 20,000 comes from memory, measured in Node: one Submit holds 56 MB at 20,000 captures and 111 MB at 40,000, and one isolate has 128 MB for all its requests. The number is a setting of the service, and a measurement in a Worker must confirm it. The review page cannot keep its code, because it would hold 119 MB at 20,000 captures. Your answer to D-RUN-02 changes the same read. At about 19 more captures each day, the suite has 20,000 captures in about 2.3 years. But one new dimension in Ariakit, for example a second viewport for each screenshot, doubles the count in one day. The D1 writes are the same. For Ariakit: one pull request with the new versions of the CLI and of the capture adapter. With your answer to D-OPS-04, the service then needs no new pinned values. The baseline needs the new form one time, and older runs lose their capture list. Line 26 of the contract changes from one object to one index with its pages. Not built: the CLI part, and the manifest digest as a digest of the page digests. Effort L. To reverse it, use the earlier CLI version and import the baseline again.

options.label: Pages of rows, and each reader works page by page now
options.explanation: The option above, and no step of the service holds the complete list. Submit validation and materialization walk the pages of the run and of the baseline together, because both are in the same order. Promotion, the recovery check, and the history export handle one page in each step.
options.consequences: The capture list no longer limits a run. Measured in Node: one step holds about 26 MB at most, at 100,000 and at 500,000 captures. A run of 100,000 captures is 50 pages and 41.7 MB. A run of 500,000 is 250 pages and 224 MB. The D1 writes are the same. But 8 other limits stop a run before it has more than 100,000 captures: limits of a capture job, constants of the CLI, and settings of the service. Each needs its own change. It is the largest change: a rewrite of Submit validation and materialization, which are the steps that check if a run can be trusted, and of promotion and recovery. Nothing of it is built. Effort XL. For Ariakit it is the same one pull request as the option above.

settledAnswer: The CLI sends the captures as rows, 2,000 in each page, in the order of the item name and the variant name. The service stores pages of rows and one page index, and D1 points to the index. The review page reads the unchanged captures one page at a time. Submit validation, materialization, promotion, and the recovery check keep their code in this step, and the service refuses a run above about 20,000 captures with a clear reason. When a suite comes near that number, these steps change to work on one page at a time, with no change of the format, of the CLI, or of Ariakit.
rationale: The maintainer selected it in round 3. The note asked for the most scalable form, for hundreds of thousands of screenshots. Pages of short rows are that form: 100,000 captures are 50 objects of about 0.8 MB, where the records of today are 320 MB (prototype). The 3,832 captures of today are 2 pages and an index of 913 bytes in place of one object of 12.15 MB. No D1 write is added. The format and the CLI requests change now, in one pull request in Ariakit, because only those parts need a change in Ariakit. The limit of about 20,000 captures for one run is a setting of the service and not an approved number: it comes from Node (one Submit holds 56 MB at 20,000 captures, and one isolate has 128 MB), and the earlier decision D54 asks for a measurement in a Worker first. On 2026-10-07 the maintainer authorized the implementation. So the measurement is a task of the implementation, and the maintainer approves the number in the contract pull request that states it. The review page must read one page at a time from the start, which is the same read that D-RUN-02 changes. With D-OPS-04 settled as the OIDC token with no file check, the new versions of the CLI and of the capture adapter need no pinned value in the service after that cutover. The baseline needs the new form one time, and older runs lose their capture list. Line 26 of the contract changes from one object to one index with its pages. Not built: the CLI part, and the manifest digest as a digest of the page digests. The maintainer said on 2026-10-07 that 'hundreds of thousands of screenshots' means one run of that size. question: Does each run of a suite with hundreds of thousands of captures capture every screenshot?
context: You said on 2026-10-07 that one run can have hundreds of thousands of captures. The service accepts only a complete run today. With the CI medians of today (4.67 captures each second on Linux, 1.94 on Safari), one run of 300,000 captures needs about 26 hours of capture jobs, and Ariakit has 15 to 23 runs each day. GitHub gives a Free, Pro, or Team plan 5 macOS jobs at the same time. No option is recommended: the answer needs your plan for the suite and for its runners, and the two partial options are not designed.

options.label: Each run captures every screenshot
options.explanation: No change of the contract. Ariakit adds capture jobs and raises the job timeouts. The CLI gets higher constants.
options.consequences: The service work is the order of the part 'One run of hundreds of thousands of captures' and nothing more. The capture time is a cost of Ariakit: 8.6, 25.7, and 42.9 hours of job time for one run of 100,000, 300,000, and 500,000 captures (estimate). With the run rate and the browser mix of today, 5 macOS jobs that do nothing else make the Safari captures of runs of 116,000 to 178,000 captures at most. Above that, Ariakit needs another GitHub plan, its own runners, fewer Safari captures, or fewer runs. Each new capture job needs a matrix entry in the workflow file, and its name and its exact command in the Playwright configuration of Ariakit. Reversible.

options.label: A run can capture a part of the suite
options.explanation: The Submit job names the tests that it captured. The service takes each other capture from the baseline as unchanged.
options.consequences: The capture time follows the size of the change. It changes the rule that a run is complete: a pull request can leave out the screenshot that it breaks, so the service needs a rule that says which tests a commit must capture, and who decides that. Today a capture of the baseline that a run does not have is a removal, so that rule also changes. Not designed and not measured. Effort XL.

options.label: Complete runs on main, partial runs on pull requests
options.explanation: A pull request run captures the tests that its change selects. Each main run captures every screenshot, so the baseline always comes from a complete run.
options.consequences: A screenshot that a pull request left out is found by the main run, after the merge and not before it. The main runs keep the capture time of a complete run. It needs the same selection rule as the option before. Not designed and not measured. Effort XL.

settledAnswer: Each run captures every screenshot, and the contract does not change. The capture time of a larger suite is a later optimization. The record designs no partial run now.
rationale: The maintainer selected it in round 4 with the note “We'll optimize capture later. No need to think about this now.” The service work for a larger run is then the order of the part “One run of hundreds of thousands of captures” and nothing more. The capture time stays a cost of Ariakit: 8.6, 25.7, and 42.9 hours of job time for one run of 100,000, 300,000, and 500,000 captures (estimate from the CI medians of today). With the run rate and the browser mix of today, 5 macOS jobs at the same time make the Safari captures of runs of 116,000 to 178,000 captures at most. The question is not urgent: one Linux job makes 33,600 captures in its 120 minutes, and step 1 of D-DATA-02 accepts about 20,000. A partial run stays possible later. It changes what the required check proves, so it needs its own research before it is an answer.

short: A run with a mass change
question: What does the service do with a run in which more captures changed than one transaction and one review can hold?
context: A browser update, a font change, or a shared style can change every capture of a run. A new capture is also a change: the first run of a new project has only changes, and a new viewport for each screenshot doubles a suite in one run. Today that is 3,832 changes at most. The code has no limit of changes: four steps write rows for each change in one transaction (measured on a local D1: 5 rows for the run approval of D-WORK-04, 8 for the closed summary, 6 for the release; the finalize step copies approvals in the same way). The limits page of D1 says that a statement that writes hundreds of thousands of rows exceeds the execution limits, and that one database runs one query at a time. 30,000 changes are 150,008 rows for the run approval and 240,024 for the closed summary. A local D1 accepted these, and also 1.5 million rows for 300,000 changes. Nobody tested production D1. The first option is recommended because it is the smallest change and it refuses before the uploads.

options.label: A stated limit of changes for one run
options.explanation: The service gets a setting for the changed captures of one run, for example 20,000. When the CLI declares more, the service refuses the run before the uploads, with a reason that names the limit. After a mass change, a maintainer makes the new baseline with the import tool.
options.consequences: Each settled answer holds as it is: the run approval stays one transaction, and the first response needs pages only above some thousand changes. The limit is also the largest count of new captures in one run: a suite grows by that count for each merge, and the first baseline of a large new project comes from the import tool. A pull request with a mass change gets a failed check with a clear text, and it cannot pass review in the service: a maintainer imports the baseline, or the author splits the change. The import tool accepts 10,000 captures today and must learn the pages of D-DATA-02. The number of the limit needs one measurement on production D1, for the closed summary (8 rows for each change) and for the run approval. Effort M. To reverse it, raise the setting.

options.label: Each step works in parts, for any count
options.explanation: The uploads, the D1 rows, the finalize step, the run approval, the closed summary, and the release work in parts of a fixed size. The run approval becomes several transactions with a state 'approval in progress'.
options.consequences: A run with any count of changes can pass review. It changes the words 'in one transaction' of your answer to D-WORK-04: an approval can stop in the middle, so it needs a rule to continue and a rule for Undo of a part. D1 still gets rows for each change: 31 at Submit, 5 for the decision, and 14 after 30 days. So one run of 300,000 changes writes about 15 million rows, which is 30% of the 50 million that the plan includes each month, and it adds 2.2 GB to a database that refuses new runs at 2 GiB. So it also needs your answer to D-SCALE-03 and a capacity stop above 2 GiB. The Submit job uploads 600,000 images, 5 at the same time: not measured. Effort L to XL.

options.label: Above the limit, one decision for the run and no row for each change
options.explanation: Below the limit nothing changes. Above it, the changed captures of the run stay in its capture pages only, D1 gets no row for each change, and the only decisions are Approve run and Reject run, each as one row.
options.consequences: The fewest D1 writes: 66 rows for the run and about 21 for the decision. It is the option 'run approval with one row' of D-WORK-04, which you did not select, for large runs only: each part of the code that reads decisions needs a second rule (11 source files), a later run copies no approval from it, and no row says who approved one variant. The review page shows such a run from the pages, with no decision for one screenshot. The uploads are the same as in the option before. Not built. Effort XL.

settledAnswer: When a run with a mass change becomes a problem, the answer is a stated limit of changed captures for one run: the service refuses such a run before the uploads, with a reason that names the limit, and a maintainer makes the new baseline with the import tool. Nothing is built for it now.
rationale: The maintainer selected the limit in round 4 with the note “Let's defer this to when this is a problem.” The record reads the selection and the note together: the form is decided, and the work waits. A note can change that reading. Until then the code has no limit of changes, and each settled answer holds as it is. With step 1 of D-DATA-02 a run has at most about 20,000 captures, so a run in which every capture changed writes 100,008 rows for one run approval and 160,024 rows for the closed summary, each in one transaction (formulas measured on a local D1: 5 and 8 rows for each change). Nobody tested production D1 at that size, and the largest run of today has 3,832 captures. The number of the limit needs one measurement on production D1. That measurement writes rows. The maintainer authorized it on 2026-10-07, and it waits with the limit. When the limit is built: the limit is also the largest count of new captures in one run, and the import needs a new path. The import tool of today copies an accepted baseline from one database into another database that has no run (apps/web/tooling/baseline-reset/reset.ts:150-198), so it cannot take the captures of a refused run, and a new project has no baseline to copy. The effort M of the option does not have that path. The refusal also needs its own error code, so that the wait of D-OPS-05 does not apply to it. To reverse it, raise the setting.

question: What happens to the D1 rows of the changed captures of a closed run?
context: Your answer to D-DATA-04 deletes the images of replaced baselines after 30 days and keeps the rows. Measured on a local D1 with rows of production length and the steps of the product: one changed capture has 7.4 KB with its decision. 30 days after its run closed, the code of today deletes its capture row and its 2 image rows, and it writes 2 copies (one of the changed row, one of the decision) for the history of the run. Then 9.1 KB stay, with no end. Today that is about 30 KB for a run with 4 changed captures. With runs of 300,000 captures and 1% changed captures in each, the database grows by 10 to 15 GB in the first 30 days: it reaches the capacity stop of 2 GiB in 4 to 6 days (estimate). D-DATA-04 had the option 'Give each class an end', which you did not select. It did not name these rows. The second option is recommended, for the time of step 2 of D-DATA-02 and not before.

options.label: Keep the rows
options.explanation: D-DATA-04 stays as you answered it. The capacity stop moves up when the database comes near it.
options.consequences: No code and no write. The limit is the 10 GB of one D1 database, which Cloudflare does not raise: about 1.1 million changed captures at 9.1 KB, in all runs together. For the suite of today that is far: 16 to 25 MB each month. With 100,000 captures and 0.1% changed captures in each run it is 16 to 24 months. With 300,000 captures and 1% it is one month or less. The statements that count the changes of a run read more rows as the rows stay.

options.label: Delete the rows of a closed run with its images
options.explanation: After the 30-day window, the step that deletes the images of a closed run also deletes its changed rows and its decisions, in parts of a fixed size, and it writes no copy. The run row, its counts, and its capture pages in R2 stay. A run that is the baseline, or that a later run still needs, is not released, as in D-DATA-04.
options.consequences: The database then holds the changed captures of about 30 days and of the baselines. That is enough while the runs of 30 days have fewer than about 1.3 million changed captures together: 2,000 to 3,000 for each run at the run rate of today. With 1% of 300,000 in each run it is not enough, and the window for rows must then be shorter than 30 days. The code of today already writes 14 rows for each changed capture, one time, 30 days after the run closed (measured). A deletion in place of the 2 copies is not measured. A closed run older than 30 days shows its counts and its capture list, and no decision for one variant: the name of the reviewer of a single variant is lost. An approval older than the window is not copied to a later run. Check two things first: a comment in the code says that the kept rows 'still serve baseline and source approval checks' (closed-summary.ts:315), and the earlier decision D14 forbids a row deletion for retired data. Deleted rows do not come back. Effort M to L.

options.label: Move the rows of a closed run to R2
options.explanation: After the window, the service writes the changed rows and the decisions of a closed run as one object beside its capture pages, in place of the 2 copies in D1, and then deletes the D1 rows as in the option before.
options.consequences: The history of a closed run stays complete: who decided which variant. More code than the option before: a writer, a reader for the history page, and a digest check. The same limit for the rows of the first 30 days, and the same two checks first. Effort L.

settledAnswer: After the 30-day window, the step that deletes the images of a closed run also deletes its changed rows and its decisions in D1, in parts of a fixed size, and it writes no copy. The run row, its counts, and its capture pages in R2 stay. A run that is the baseline, or that a later run still needs, is not released. The change comes with step 2 of D-DATA-02, and not before.
rationale: The maintainer selected it in round 4 with no note, so the time that the record recommended stays: with step 2 of D-DATA-02. One D1 database has a hard limit of 10 GB. The code of today keeps 9.1 KB for each changed capture with no end (measured on a local D1 with the steps of the product), which is 16 to 25 MB each month for the suite of today. With the deletion, the database holds the changed captures of about 30 days and of the baselines. That is enough while the runs of 30 days have fewer than about 1.3 million changed captures together. What it gives up: a closed run older than 30 days shows its counts and its capture list and no decision for one variant, so the name of the reviewer of a single variant is lost, and an approval older than the window is not copied to a later run. It changes the answer to D-DATA-04 for rows (“Inventories and bookkeeping rows stay”) contract line 33 (the decisions and approval tuples of closed runs “remain readable”), and the earlier decision D05 (“Preserve original decisions, exact tuples”). A deletion is a one-time write for each closed run, which the rule on D1 writes accepts, and it replaces the 14 rows that the code of today writes for each changed capture after 30 days.
