short: Image files that no program checked
question: A pull request can now replace the job that checks each screenshot file. Must the service check the files itself before it stores them?
context: Each screenshot is a PNG file. One program opens each file and confirms that it is a real PNG of the stated size: the CLI (visonaut submit) in the Submit job of ariakit/ariakit. The service does not open the file. It compares only the number of bytes and the SHA-256 digest with the list that the same job sent. You answered D-CODE-02 (remove the comparison Worker) when a pinned workflow file fixed the Submit job. With your answer to D-OPS-04, one of the 5 accounts with push access can replace that job in a pull request. Example: such a job sends 2 MiB of text as the screenshot dialog/open. The service stores it and serves it as image/png. The tables above this panel show what each check stops. No option adds a D1 write, and no option needs a CLI release.

options.label: 1. No new check: keep the size and the digest
options.explanation: Nothing is built. The service keeps the two checks of today. The contract then says it in plain words: the CLI in the Submit job checks each image, and the service checks only the size and the digest.
options.consequences: Cost: no code and no CPU time. In a pull request with a replaced Submit job, the service stores each file of 2 MiB or less and serves it as image/png at a public address. A browser runs nothing from it (measured in 3 browsers). A reviewer who opens a text file, or a PNG with a false size in its header, sees an error and cannot approve it (3 browsers). A reviewer who opens a damaged PNG sees an empty or partial picture and can approve it (Chromium and WebKit). An approval of the run can cover a file that nobody opened (your answer to D-WORK-04). All of this stays in that pull request. The worst case needs a second failure: the replaced job is merged to main (1 approval and a code owner review). A bad file can then enter the baseline, and each later Submit with that screenshot fails where the CLI decodes the baseline image, in each pull request, until someone repairs the baseline. Nobody tested a repair. To reverse: add a check below in one service deployment. Files stored before that stay unchecked. Answer this again before a second customer (rule 5): its accounts with push access are not your team.

options.label: 2. Read the PNG header: 33 bytes
options.explanation: Before the write to R2, the upload code reads the first 33 bytes of each image: the PNG signature, and the width and the height in the header. It refuses the upload when they differ from the declared values. It does not read the image data.
options.consequences: Cost: about 15 lines in uploadStagedImage and their tests (estimate). Below 0.01 ms for each uploaded image (measured in Node, not in a Worker). No more memory. Refuses: bytes that are not a PNG, and a PNG whose header declares another size, for example 30,000 by 30,000 pixels. These are the two kinds of file that the review page already refuses. The difference: the service refuses them before it stores them, also when no reviewer opens them. Accepts: a damaged PNG, a PNG that is cut after 4,000 bytes (both measured), and each file that starts with a correct header. An honest run gets no new failure, because the CLI compares the same values. The contract can then say: the service checks the size, the digest, and the PNG header. The check does not depend on who has push access (rule 5). To reverse: delete the lines.

options.label: 3. Parse the PNG structure in the web Worker

question: Which checks must pass between a merge and the production deploy?
context: The deploy workflow runs the full suite again: 380 of 433 s in the measured run. The branch rule of main does not require an up-to-date branch, so for some merges this second run is the only test of the merged tree. In 71 of the last 100 merges it is a repeat: the merge commit has the same tree as the last commit of the pull request. The recommended option removes only these repeats.

options.label: Run the full suite again
options.explanation: Today. Each push to main runs all checks and then deploys.
options.consequences: A change is live 257 s after the merge (median of 67 deploys; maximum 451 s). Each merged tree is tested, also when the pull request ran on an older base. This is the state that earlier decision D11 records.

options.label: Skip the suite for a tree that passed
options.explanation: A first job compares the Git tree of the merge commit with the tree of the last commit of the pull request, whose required checks passed. If they are equal, deploy. If they differ, or if the job cannot tell, run the full suite as today.
options.consequences: The second run goes away for 71 of the last 100 merges: 366 s in the measured run. The rule stays: a merged tree is tested before deploy. D11 keeps job dependencies "unless evidence supports a later change", and this count is that evidence. Nobody built the job. It needs read access to the pull request and its checks, and the release guards that read deploy.yml as text change with it. Effort M. One commit reverts it.

options.label: Use a merge queue
options.explanation: GitHub runs the checks on the merge group, so main gets only tested commits. The deploy workflow runs no checks.
options.consequences: This reopens earlier decision D11 ("No branch-rule edit is authorized"). Each merge waits for one CI run in the queue (median 294 s now), so a change is not live sooner than today (estimate: 294 s plus the deploy job of 50 s). It changes how each pull request merges, also the "Version packages" pull request. The busiest measured day had 33 deploys. You can revert the rule and the merge_group trigger.

options.label: Run only the short jobs again
options.explanation: On main, run lint, type check, build, and release guards (the longest is 49 s). Then deploy and read /health.
options.consequences: With the present branch rule, a merged tree that never passed the tests can go to production: in 29 of the last 100 merges, the tree differs from the last commit of the pull request. The check after deploy finds a Worker that does not start, not a D1 failure, because /health is static. It changes a job dependency that D11 keeps, and it is near D12 ("Do not add a second automated smoke project").

settledAnswer: A first job of the deploy workflow compares the Git tree of the merge commit with the tree of the last commit of the pull request, and when they are equal and the required checks passed, the deploy starts with no second run of the suite. If they differ, or if the job cannot tell, the full suite runs as today.
rationale: In 71 of the last 100 merges the merge commit has the same tree as the last commit of the pull request, and the second run is 380 of 433 s. The rule stays: a merged tree is tested before deploy. Nobody built the job, and the release guards that read deploy.yml as text change with it.

short: The promise about an unsaved decision
question: What does the page promise about a decision that the server stored and did not process yet?
context: The maintainer selected server storage for pending decisions, with processing after the window closes (docs/current-contract.md, line 196), and the server does that. The same line says that failed commands “remain visible through their receipts”. The server keeps each receipt, but no screen can find one after a reload, because the command ID is in React state only. No option is recommended: the choice depends on what that sentence means, a rule for the page or a rule for the server data, and on how often a queued decision fails after the page is gone, which no lane measured. If the sentence is a rule for the page, the second option is the smallest one that obeys it.

options.label: Keep the sentence, change nothing
options.explanation: The decision bar says “You can close this window.” after HTTP 202. A reload forgets each queued decision, as today.
options.consequences: No cost. The gap needs a reload or a close in the time before the receipt, or a fault of the processing. In that time a queued decision shows as “Needs review” after a reload, and a second decision for that variant ends in a conflict. A decision that fails after a close shows nowhere; it changes no verdict, so the harm is a decision that the reviewer must make again. The contract sentence then holds for the server data only.

options.label: Remember the command IDs in the browser
options.explanation: At HTTP 202, the page writes the run, the command ID, the variant, and the verdict to localStorage. On each load it reads those receipts, and it shows the decisions that are pending or that the server did not apply.
options.consequences: Client code only: no new endpoint and no migration. No contract change. It works in one browser profile: another device shows nothing. An entry must go when its receipt is final or when the server answers 404, or the page shows a pending decision that does not exist. options.label: List the receipts from the server
options.explanation: A new read returns the queued and the failed decisions of the reviewer for one run. The page shows them after each load, on each device.
options.consequences: A new endpoint and a new index: no index fits this read today, so it would scan the review tasks. It adds one read to each run load, or more data to a run model that is slow today. No contract change. The index is a migration, so this option is the hardest to reverse.

options.label: Remove the sentence, wait for the receipt
options.explanation: The decision bar says “Saving…” until the receipt is final. The leave prompt stays on until then.
options.consequences: A small client change with no storage. It reopens the visible half of the earlier decision in contract line 196, and line 21 of the review guide changes: the server continues after a close, but the page does not say so. Each close during a save asks for confirmation. A reload continues to forget a queued decision.

question: Does the page save a review decision through the decision queue, or directly in one request?

options.explanation: No change. The page sends each decision with queued: true. The server stores a task row, answers HTTP 202, and processes the decision after that answer. The page polls for the decision receipt.
options.consequences: Keeps: a decision that the server stored survives a closed tab, and the server processes fast decisions in their order and tries a stored decision again by itself, 5 times at most. Your selected answers stay as they are: D-RUN-05, D-RES-02, row 6 of D-RES-01, the receipt read of D-RUN-01, and row 12 of D-OPS-01. Row 6 of D-RES-01 says “still queued” and D-RES-02 says “Saving…”: the two texts must become one. No contract change.

The server has this path today (review.ts, lines 879 to 904), no page calls it, and the page code already reads its answer.
options.consequences: About 14 rows written for one variant in place of 27 (estimate: the 27 measured rows minus the 13 of the task row; nobody ran this path). The conflict answer has the GitHub user ID of the reviewer who decided first; the text is that of D-RES-05, the stored name. Gives up: nothing promises a decision whose request the tab ends, so only the leave prompt of D-RES-02 protects it. The page sends one decision request at a time, so a fast second decision waits for the first answer. Not measured: the time of the request in production, and fast decisions on this path. It reverses your decision in contract line 196: the page no longer uses the queue of pull request #190. To go back, the page sends queued: true again, while the server keeps that branch.

settledAnswer: The page keeps the decision queue: it sends each decision with queued: true, the server stores a task row and answers HTTP 202, and the page polls for the receipt.
rationale: The maintainer selected it in round 2. A stored decision survives a closed tab, and the server processes fast decisions in their order and tries a stored decision again by itself. The selected answers D-RUN-05, D-RES-02, row 6 of D-RES-01, and row 12 of D-OPS-01 stay as they are. The cost stays as today: 27 rows written for one decision for one variant, 13 of them for the task row (local D1). short: How an open run page learns about changes
question: How does an open run page learn that a newer run, another reviewer, or a sign-out changed the state?
context: Today a ready run page reads one time, and the first sign of a change is a failed save. D-UX-05 (UI structure section) asks the same question for the run list and recommends a refresh on focus and on a slow interval. The run page differs in two ways: each decision is a save, and a save returns the current state; and the state answer cannot show the decision of another reviewer without one new field. Thus the second option is recommended: it closes the verified gap with a pattern that the code has. The timer adds one case only, a run that changes below a page that stays in front with no save. No lane measured how often that occurs.

options.label: Only when a save fails
options.explanation: No read between load and save, as today. The no-regret list corrects the texts that follow the failed save.
options.consequences: No new request. A reviewer who returns to an old tab reads the screenshots of a replaced run until the next decision. A sign-out in another tab shows only at the next request.

options.label: Read when the tab returns
options.explanation: When the tab becomes visible, the page makes one state read. It reads the run model again only when the state changed.
options.consequences: One state read for each return. It finds a replaced run. A 401 on that read shows a sign-out in another tab, and D-AUTH-03 decides what the page then does. To find the decision of another reviewer, the state answer needs one new field, the run revision. A page that stays in front learns at the next save, as today. No contract change. Reversible: remove one listener.

options.label: Read on return and on a slow timer
options.explanation: The option before, and one state read each 30 to 60 s while the page is visible. This is the rule of the option “Refresh on focus and on a slow interval” of D-UX-05.
options.consequences: One rule for the lists and for the run page. A visible page learns in one interval at most. Each visible run page adds 60 to 120 requests in one hour, and each request passes the access check. The server time of a state read is not measured. No contract change. Reversible: remove one timer.

settledAnswer: When the tab of an open run page becomes visible, the page makes one state read. It reads the run model again only when the state changed.
rationale: It closes the verified gap with a pattern that the code has, for one state read on each return. It finds a replaced run and a sign-out in another tab. To find the decision of another reviewer, the state answer needs one new field, the run revision, and a page that stays in front learns at the next save, as today.

The name is the GitHub profile name at the first sign-in, or the login when the profile has no name. It does not follow a later change on GitHub, and two people can have the same name. options.label: Add a login at sign-in

question: Which browsers must the review flow support?

short: Old UI rules of the contract
